vecchio: At 1.3 million cells, the 8-GPU pipeline completed the full analysis in 435.2 +/- 16.2 s (7.3 min), compared with 52,056.2 +/- 392.0 s (14.5 h) for the CPU pipeline, a 119.6-fold speedup.
nuovo: At 1.3 million cells, the GPU pipeline with eight GPUs allocated completed the full analysis in 435.2 +/- 16.2 s (7.3 min), compared with 52,056.2 +/- 392.0 s (14.5 h) for the CPU pipeline, a 119.6-fold speedup. With two GPUs allocated the time was 493.3 +/- 10.3 s (105.5-fold); the difference lies in data loading (149.0 against 90.6 s, runs on different nodes), because the additional GPUs did not take part in the computation. Wilcoxon differential expression accounted for 93.5% of the CPU time (48,688.3 s of 52,056.2 s); without it the speedup was 7.9-fold with two GPUs and 9.2-fold with eight. Dicks et al. report, on the 10x Genomics mouse brain dataset and with differential expression and I/O excluded, more than 120-fold on one B200 GPU and 110-fold on one H200 GPU against a 32-core workstation CPU [@Dicks2026]; in our hybrid pipeline a similar end-to-end factor arises mainly from the CPU Wilcoxon test.

vecchio: However, not all operations benefited equally from GPU acceleration. Data loading from disk was actually faster on CPU across all scales (0.76-0.85x GPU/CPU), because the fixed overhead of CUDA context initialisation and RMM pool allocation dominated the short data transfer itself: PCIe Gen5 bandwidth (128 GB/s) is not saturated at these sub-gigabyte dataset sizes, and the transfer completes in milliseconds. We note that our pipeline relies on `h5py`-based readers that route data through CPU RAM, precluding GPU Direct Storage (GDS) optimisations that would bypass the CPU entirely; this remains an avenue for future improvement. Similarly, Leiden clustering showed a clear dependence on problem size: at 10k cells, CPU was faster (0.36x) due to cuGraph's higher constant-time overhead for graph partitioning operations on small graphs, but GPU performance improved substantially as the graph size increased, with GPU overtaking CPU at 50k cells (1.80x speedup) and achieving 3.58x speedup at 100k cells.
nuovo: However, not all operations benefited equally from GPU acceleration. Data loading was slightly slower on GPU at all three sizes (0.76-0.85x, CPU time divided by GPU time). The GPU timer covers reading the file and copying the matrix to the device (`anndata_to_GPU`), whereas CUDA context creation and RMM pool allocation happen before the timer starts; the GPU excess grew with dataset size (0.10 s at 10k, 0.55 s at 50k and 1.38 s at 100k cells), so it is a size-dependent transfer cost rather than a fixed overhead. We note that our pipeline relies on `h5py`-based readers that route data through CPU RAM, precluding GPU Direct Storage (GDS) optimisations that would bypass the CPU entirely; this remains an avenue for future improvement. For Leiden clustering at resolution 0.5, the CPU was faster at 10k cells (0.36x), but this reflects the first Leiden call of the first repeat (1.70 s against 0.09 to 0.23 s in later repeats); at resolutions 1.0 and 1.5 the GPU was already faster at 10k cells (1.36x and 1.60x). At resolution 0.5 the GPU was 1.80x faster at 50k and 3.58x faster at 100k cells. The first repeat of each configuration includes one-off library loading and compilation on both CPU and GPU, and it sets the extreme per-step values at 10k cells: excluding it, normalisation was 115.1x faster on GPU (instead of 329x) and Leiden at resolution 0.5 was 1.12x faster (instead of 0.36x). End-to-end speedups changed by at most 6% from 100k cells upwards.

nuovo: ### Multi-GPU configuration

vecchio: Adding GPUs beyond two provided diminishing returns (Fig. 3).
nuovo: At 500k and 1.3M cells only the hybrid Dask-CUDA pipeline could run. In the configuration used, the expression matrix was passed to PCA and neighbour search as a CuPy array on one device, so these steps ran on a single GPU whatever the number of GPUs allocated: PCA plus neighbour search took 17.23, 16.99 and 17.01 s with 2, 4 and 8 GPUs at 1.3M cells, and 2.98, 2.97 and 3.00 s at 500k cells, where total wall time was 124.5, 125.0 and 124.6 s. At 1.3M cells the 8-GPU run (435.2 s) was 12% faster than the 2-GPU run (493.3 s), but the difference arose in CPU-side data loading (149.0 s against 90.6 s), the jobs ran concurrently, and the 8-GPU job ran on a different node. The aggregate VRAM of the multi-GPU runs reflects the RMM pools pre-allocated by the Dask workers (78.6 GiB added at cluster start-up with 8 GPUs, at 10k as at 1.3M cells), not distributed data. Multi-GPU scaling was therefore not measured. Between 10k and 100k cells the 2-GPU hybrid pipeline was 49-82% slower than the single-GPU pipeline, because it runs preprocessing on the CPU.

vecchio: Concordance analysis on the 10,000-cell dataset (Fig. 5) demonstrated that the two pipelines yield near-identical biological conclusions, despite computing on different processors and hardware. Upstream analysis steps showed deterministic agreement: HVG selection was perfectly concordant with all 2,000 genes identical between CPU and GPU (Jaccard = 1.000), and PCA loadings were perfectly correlated with mean absolute Spearman rho = 1.000 across all 10 inspected principal components. Neighbourhood graph construction achieved high overlap with mean Jaccard = 0.930 (median = 0.938), though some variation in the k-nearest neighbours across the graph was expected due to floating-point precision differences.
nuovo: Concordance analysis on the 10,000-cell dataset (Fig. 5) demonstrated that the two pipelines yield closely agreeing outputs, despite computing on different processors and hardware. Concordance was computed on a separate pair of 10,000-cell runs made on 11 March 2026 (UTC), before the timed benchmark; in that run the CPU pipeline found 31, 40 and 45 clusters at resolutions 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5, against 31, 41 and 46 in all five benchmark repeats. Upstream analysis steps showed deterministic agreement: HVG selection was perfectly concordant with all 2,000 genes identical between CPU and GPU (Jaccard = 1.000), and PCA loadings were perfectly correlated with mean absolute Spearman rho = 1.000 across all 10 inspected principal components. Neighbourhood graph construction achieved high overlap with mean Jaccard = 0.930 (median = 0.938). This value is bounded by construction: the CPU and GPU neighbour sets compared have different sizes (the maximum and the median per-cell Jaccard are both 0.9375 = 15/16, and no cell reaches 1), so at least half of the cells reach that maximum and differ only by the size mismatch. In the saved neighbour lists of the benchmark runs at 10,000 cells, identical in all five repeats, each cell has 16 CPU and 15 GPU neighbour indices, the cell itself included, and for 95.0% of cells every GPU neighbour is also a CPU neighbour. The remaining differences are consistent with approximate neighbour search on CPU (PyNNDescent, the Scanpy default at this size) against exact brute-force search on GPU [@Gardner2025], rather than with floating-point precision.

vecchio: Clustering concordance showed expected variations due to algorithm stochasticity. Leiden clustering at different resolutions yielded adjusted Rand indices ranging from 0.908 (resolution 1.0) to 0.963 (resolution 1.5), with corresponding normalised mutual information values from 0.951 to 0.971. The slightly lower concordance at resolution 1.0, where both pipelines identified 40 clusters, reflects the inherent stochasticity of the Leiden algorithm and minor differences in the underlying graph-partitioning implementations provided by cuGraph (GPU) versus igraph (CPU), rather than indicating any systematic bias. The downstream biological results also aligned well: differential expression log-fold-changes across 40 matched cluster pairs showed mean Spearman correlation of 0.946, with 30 of the 40 pairs exceeding the stringent threshold of rho > 0.97.
nuovo: Clustering concordance was high but not perfect. Leiden clustering at different resolutions yielded adjusted Rand indices ranging from 0.908 (resolution 1.0) to 0.963 (resolution 1.5), with corresponding normalised mutual information values from 0.951 to 0.971. The lower agreement at resolution 1.0 (40 clusters in both pipelines in the concordance run) does not reflect run-to-run stochasticity: at 10,000 cells each pipeline returned identical labels in all five benchmark repeats. It reflects differences between the two pipelines, which include the neighbour graph (above) and the Leiden implementation: igraph with `n_iterations=2` on CPU and cuGraph with up to 100 iterations on GPU. The downstream biological results also aligned well: differential expression log-fold-changes across 40 matched cluster pairs showed mean Spearman correlation of 0.946 (median 0.9995; the mean is lowered by two pairs, one of which shares no cells), with 34 of the 40 pairs above rho = 0.97.

vecchio: These concordance levels are consistent with the range of inter-method variation reported in mixture-control benchmarks of scRNA-seq analysis pipelines [@Tian2019] and systematic evaluations of clustering algorithm variability [@Duo2020], and support the conclusion that GPU and CPU pipelines are interchangeable for biological interpretation.
nuovo: At 10,000 cells the two pipelines therefore agreed closely. This does not establish interchangeability at atlas scale: from 50,000 cells upwards GPU Leiden labels varied across the five repeats at one or more resolutions despite a fixed seed, whereas CPU labels did not, and a comparison of Scanpy and rapids-singlecell on the 1.3-million-cell mouse brain data and its subsamples reported CPU-GPU ARI near 0.5 and concluded that the two are not interchangeable [@Gardner2025].

vecchio: At the scales covered by the main benchmark (10k to 1.3M cells), neither memory tier was saturated. CPU RAM usage scaled approximately linearly with cell count, from 1.2 GB at 10k to 107.4 GB at 1.3M cells (Fig. 6, left panel), well below 6% of the 2 TB system memory. The dominant in-memory objects at 1.3M cells were the dense float32 matrix created during scaling (1.3M x 2,000 HVGs x 4 bytes approximately  10.4 GB) and the sparse raw count matrix (1.3M x 39,182 genes). GPU VRAM for single-GPU runs was approximately constant at 40.7 GB across dataset sizes, dominated by the pre-allocated RMM pool. For multi-GPU runs, aggregate VRAM scaled with worker count: at 1.3M cells with 8 GPUs, the aggregate peak was 134.2 GB (mean 16.8 GB per device, 21% of 80 GB capacity), well below the per-device limit. At these scales, therefore, end-to-end throughput is set by compute and I/O, not memory; CPU RAM becomes the binding constraint only in the extreme stress-test regime discussed in the next subsection.
nuovo: At the scales covered by the main benchmark (10k to 1.3M cells), neither memory tier was saturated. CPU RAM grew roughly in proportion to cell count (log-log slope 0.92 over 10k-1.3M cells, least squares on the five mean peaks; steeper, 1.35, between 500k and 1.3M cells), from 1.2 GiB at 10k to 107.4 GiB at 1.3M cells (Fig. 6, left panel), well below 6% of the 2 TB system memory. The dominant in-memory objects at 1.3M cells were the dense float32 matrix created during scaling (1.3M x 2,000 HVGs x 4 bytes, approximately 9.7 GiB) and the sparse raw count matrix (1.3M x 39,182 genes). GPU VRAM for single-GPU runs was approximately constant at 40.7 GiB across dataset sizes, dominated by the pre-allocated RMM pool. For multi-GPU runs, aggregate VRAM grew with the number of Dask workers, each of which pre-allocates an RMM pool (134.2 GiB with 8 GPUs at 1.3M cells, averaged over five repeats). At these scales neither memory tier limited the runs; CPU memory was pushed further only in the stress test described in the next subsection.

vecchio: To verify that distributed computation was actually occurring across all workers (rather than silently collapsing onto a single GPU, as reported for some Dask-CUDA configurations), two independent pieces of evidence support the multi-GPU claim. First, the aggregate peak VRAM at 1.3M cells with 8 GPUs (134.2 GB) exceeds the 80 GB capacity of any single H100 device; this working set could not have fit on one GPU alone, so data must have been distributed across at least two devices. Second, we verified through direct scheduler queries (`client.run_on_scheduler()`) that all requested workers were in the `running` state throughout each benchmark, after identifying and fixing a reporting bug in the client-side cache (`client.scheduler_info()`) that occasionally undercounted active workers. Per-device VRAM traces (available in the benchmark result JSON files in the code repository) show balanced usage across workers during the PCA and neighbour phases and fall back to a single-GPU footprint only during Leiden and UMAP, which are implemented as single-GPU operations in cuGraph 26.2.

vecchio: A binary search for the maximum processable cell count (Table 5) showed that the pipeline succeeded at 11.9 million cells (119 min) and failed at 12.0 million cells (Leiden out-of-memory, SLURM signal 9). nuovo: A binary search for the maximum processable cell count (Table 5) showed that the pipeline succeeded at 11.9 million cells (119 min). Above 3,436,470 cells the input was built by concatenating whole copies of the source dataset plus a random remainder, so these runs contain duplicated cells; the construction happens between data loading and QC and is not timed. "Pass" therefore denotes computational completion only: at 11.9M cells Leiden returned 135,710, 142,959 and 147,154 clusters at the three resolutions, against 58, 66 and 87 in a Leiden run on a 3,400,000-cell subset of the source dataset, a run not listed in Table 5. With this memory-optimised pipeline the single run at 12.0 million cells did not complete (the chunked variant described below completed at that size): after neighbour search had finished, the benchmark process exited with a timeout error while the Dask cluster was being shut down, before Leiden clustering started, and the job log records no out-of-memory error. Two runs at 13.7 million cells, one with Leiden and one with KMeans, were killed (signal 9) after HVG selection, while the full matrix was being copied to `adata.raw` and subset to the HVGs, before scaling.

vecchio: The failure point is counter-intuitive at first reading: the recorded peak RAM at 11.9M was 535 GB (26% of the 2 TB machine, 30% of the 1.8 TB SLURM job allocation), leaving apparent headroom, while recorded peak aggregate VRAM was only 49 GB out of 640 GB (7.6%). Neither figure explains why 12M cells fails, and our instrumentation cannot close the gap. As described in Methods, 535 GB is the largest between-step resident set size of the parent process alone. Two features of the 11.9M trace make the shortfall explicit. First, RAM rises from 124 GB at the end of data loading to 426 GB at the start of quality control, an increase of 302 GB that belongs to no timed step. Second, normalisation and HVG selection each register a between-step delta below 0.1 GB, which is possible only if their working memory is allocated and released inside the call. The step-level trace therefore records the pipeline's resting footprint between operations, not the peaks against which the SLURM cgroup enforces its limit. We report an indicative budget in Table 6 and treat the attribution of the 12M failure to a specific operation as unresolved. What the data do exclude is clustering as the CPU-side culprit: at 11.9M the three Leiden calls together added less than 1 GB of host RAM, because Leiden executes on GPU through cuGraph (aggregate VRAM rose from 28.8 GB to 48.8 GB across those calls). The 13.7M failure is a distinct event, occurring during the CPU-side sparse-to-dense scaling step.
nuovo: The recorded peak RAM at 11.9M was 535 GiB (26% of the 2 TB machine, 30% of the 1.8 TB SLURM job allocation), leaving apparent headroom, while recorded peak aggregate VRAM was only 48.8 GiB out of 640 GiB (7.6%). As described in Methods, 535 GiB is the largest between-step resident set size of the parent process alone. Two features of the 11.9M trace show what between-step sampling misses. First, RAM rises from 124 GiB at the end of data loading to 426 GiB at the start of quality control; this 302 GiB increase is the construction of the replicated 11.9M-cell dataset from the 3.4M-cell source, which runs between the two timed steps. Second, normalisation and HVG selection each register a between-step delta below 0.1 GiB, which is possible only if their working memory is allocated and released inside the call. The step-level trace therefore records the pipeline's resting footprint between operations, not the peaks against which the SLURM cgroup enforces its limit. We report an indicative budget in Table 6. At 11.9M the three Leiden calls together changed between-step host RAM by less than 1 GiB (+0.48 GiB), which, as for normalisation and HVG selection, does not exclude transient allocations within the calls; the 20 GiB rise in aggregate VRAM just before the first Leiden call occurs when the script re-initialises the RMM pool on device 0 after neighbour search, so it does not come from Leiden itself.

vecchio: ### Differential expression: pseudo-bulk is fastest and most correct
nuovo: ### Differential expression: run-time comparison

vecchio: The factorial differential expression benchmark at 3.4 million cells across 41,000 genes and 81 Leiden clusters (Table 7) revealed important trade-offs between computational efficiency and statistical rigor. To keep the table tractable we reported all wall times against a single CPU denominator, the t-test (5,598 s): a CPU Wilcoxon baseline at this scale was infeasible to measure (extrapolation from smaller subsamples places it above four hours), and pseudo-bulk operates on a different sample unit (donor x cluster pseudo-samples rather than individual cells), so no strict within-method CPU-to-GPU ratio exists for it. Consequently, the speedup column should be read as "which approach finishes fastest overall", not as a within-method GPU acceleration factor; t-test and Wilcoxon are distinct statistical tests with different computational complexity, and any direct runtime comparison between them is descriptive, not inferential.
nuovo: The factorial differential expression benchmark at 3.4 million cells across 41,000 genes and 81 Leiden clusters (Table 7) compares run times only; statistical properties of the tests were not assessed. To keep the table tractable we reported all wall times against a single CPU denominator, the t-test (5,598 s): a CPU Wilcoxon baseline was not run at this scale, and pseudo-bulk operates on a different sample unit (donor x cluster pseudo-samples rather than individual cells), so no strict within-method CPU-to-GPU ratio exists for it. Consequently, the speedup column should be read as "which approach finishes fastest overall", not as a within-method GPU acceleration factor; t-test and Wilcoxon are distinct statistical tests with different computational complexity, and any direct runtime comparison between them is descriptive, not inferential.

vecchio: Pseudo-bulk aggregation emerged as the dominant strategy: aggregating raw counts by donor and cluster reduced the analysis from 3.4 million individual cells to a few hundred pseudo-samples per cluster, completing in 128 seconds (2.1 minutes), a 43.7x speedup relative to the cell-level CPU t-test baseline (5,598 s, 93 minutes). nuovo: Pseudo-bulk aggregation was the fastest strategy: aggregating log-normalised expression by donor and cluster reduced 3.4 million cells to 2,431 pseudo-samples (about 30 per cluster), and the analysis completed in 127 s (2.1 min), 43.9 times sooner than the cell-level CPU t-test (5,598 s, 93 min). Among cell-level tests on GPU, the Wilcoxon implementation (826 s) finished sooner than the t-test (1,655 s), and multi-GPU scatter (826 s for Wilcoxon) was essentially equivalent to single-GPU chunk-and-stream (831 s).
